title: The Law Faculty and the Window: Poulantzas, the State as a Relation, and the Fall of the Dictatorships
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Vathis Square and the French Baccalaureate

stops.name: Athens, Veranzerou Street: the lawyer's son
stops.date_confidence: [A] the birthdate 21 September 1936 and the Athens birthplace are uniform across ertnews.gr, poulantzas.gr and Stuart Hall's obituary essay in New Left Review I/119; no primary vital record was located. [R] the Veranzerou Street address near Vathis Square is Jessop 1985 alone, reaching this file through a dossier summary rather than through the book, which was never opened. Coordinate corrected: the research pool plotted 37.9838/23.7278, which falls at Omonia; Nominatim places Beranzerou in the Plateia Vathis quarter at 37.9857/23.7273. [R] contradiction left standing on the father, not resolved: el.wikipedia calls Aristides a lawyer of Maniot origin, en.wikipedia a professor of forensic graphology.
stops.campa: A son is born to Aristides Poulantzas and Angeliki Kariophili in the crowded quarter north of Omonia, where lawyers and market porters share the same stairwells. They name him Nicos Aristides. Before he is five the Germans hold Athens and the famine winter empties the streets he plays in; before he is nine, Greeks are shooting Greeks in the same streets. One encyclopedia calls the father a lawyer of Maniot stock, another a professor of forensic graphology, and neither cites anything. The son will take a law degree, register with the Athens bar, and never once appear in a courtroom.
suggested_refs: Greek civil registration for the Athens birth of 21 September 1936, which would settle the date at first hand
Bob Jessop, Nicos Poulantzas: Marxist Theory and Political Strategy (Macmillan, 1985), for the Veranzerou Street address and the family background

stops.name: Athens, Skoufa Street: the Experimental School and the Institut Francais
stops.date_confidence: [A] that he attended the Peiramatikon Gymnasion of the University of Athens together with the Institut Francais d'Athenes is attested by mixanitouxronou.gr. [A] the French baccalaureate is dated to 1953 by el.wikipedia, consistent with his entering the Athens Law School the same year; the research pool's 1954 conflated the baccalaureate with the separate Salzburg episode and is corrected here. [R] 1949 is an ordering device for the start of secondary schooling and is attested by nothing; month and day defaulted. Coordinate corrected: the pool's 37.9793/23.7332 sits at the university's central building on Panepistimiou, while the Experimental School is at Skoufa 43 in Kolonaki (37.9797/23.7385) and the Institut Francais at Sina 31 one block away; this single pin covers both.
stops.campa: He is enrolled at the Peiramatikon Gymnasion, the experimental secondary school attached to the University of Athens, and one block away at the Institut Francais on Sina Street, so that his schooling runs on two tracks and in two languages at once. Neither register was opened, and what the two schools taught him in what proportion is nowhere set down. Postwar Athens is a city where the French Institute is a political fact as much as a cultural one, a room in which a defeated left can still read what Paris is printing. He sits the French baccalaureate in 1953 and enters the Athens Law School the same autumn.
suggested_refs: Registers of the Peiramatikon Gymnasion and of the Institut Francais d'Athenes for the years 1949-1953
sources: Nominatim, for Skoufa 43 and Sina 31, Athens

stops.name: Athens, Sina Street: the Law School
stops.date_confidence: [A] the law degree of 1957 with highest honours is attested by mixanitouxronou.gr; the 1953 entry is given by el.wikipedia. [R] that he entered without the ordinary entrance examination, under a French-Greek educational exchange, is Jessop 1985 alone; the research pool tagged this [A] on Stuart Hall's authority, but Hall's obituary says nothing about 1953, nothing about the Law School and nothing about an exchange waiver, and the tag is downgraded here. [A] Hall does attest the student movement and EDA, in the words quoted. Coordinate corrected: the pool labelled this Solonos Street at 37.9808/23.7328, which is the Propylaea on Panepistimiou; Nominatim puts the Law School on Sina in Kolonaki at 37.9809/23.7362. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He enters the School of Law of the University of Athens and stays four years, leaving in 1957 with a final mark of excellent. What he takes from it is not advocacy but jurisprudence, the question of where law gets its force, which will still be his question fifteen years later when he stops calling it law and starts calling it the state. Outside the lecture rooms he is in the student movement, and he joins EDA, the United Democratic Left, the legal party carrying what the Communists are banned from carrying.
stops.quote: active in the Greek student movement in the 1950's, when he joined the Greek Democratic Alliance (eda)
stops.quote_source: Stuart Hall, 'Nicos Poulantzas: State, Power, Socialism', New Left Review I/119 (January-February 1980). 'Greek Democratic Alliance' is Hall's own loose rendering of EDA, Eniaia Dimokratiki Aristera, the United Democratic Left; the expansion in the campa is the correct one and is not Hall's.
suggested_refs: University of Athens Law School matriculation and graduation records, 1953-1957
EDA membership and student-branch records for the mid-1950s
sources: Nominatim, for the Athens Law School on Sina

stops.name: Salzburg, the festival on a press card
stops.date_confidence: [R] throughout. The Salzburg trip, the press card obtained through amateur journalism for the Athens newspaper Eleftheria, and the pieces on the festival, on intellectuals and on municipal socialism all rest on Jessop 1985 as reported in the dossier; no corroborating press record was located and no issue of Eleftheria was checked. The research pool attached the French baccalaureate to this year, which is a conflation of two separate events and is corrected: the baccalaureate is 1953. Month and day are an ordering device inside the festival season and are attested by nothing. The Festspielhaus coordinate is a plausible venue pin, not a documented location for him.
stops.campa: Seventeen, carrying a press card got from amateur work for the Athens paper Eleftheria, he goes north to the Salzburg Festival and files what a young man files: notes on the music, on the intellectuals who come to hear it, and, oddly for the setting, on municipal socialism. No issue of Eleftheria from that summer has been opened, so the whole episode stands on his biographer's word. It is the first time he leaves Greece, and the route is the one his generation of Greek students takes, north and west into a Europe that has money and orchestras again.
suggested_refs: Bound volumes of Eleftheria for the summer of 1954, which would confirm or dissolve the whole episode
sources: Bob Jessop, Nicos Poulantzas: Marxist Theory and Political Strategy (1985), as summarised in the research dossier and not read directly

stops.name: Athens, arrested at a demonstration for Cyprus
stops.date_confidence: [R] the arrest is Jessop 1985 alone, via the dossier; no charge, conviction or police record is documented in any source consulted. The demonstration site is unknown and the coordinate is a central-Athens placeholder, not an attestation. Month and day defaulted. Note for the map, since the pool raised it: the atlas's existing Cyprus pins are pre-modern and have no bearing here, because this event happened in Athens about Cyprus as a political cause and not on the island.
stops.campa: The Cyprus question brings Athens into the street, and a law student is picked up in the crowd and briefly held overnight. The cause is anti-colonial and the island is British, but the demonstration is Greek and so is the policeman. No charge is entered and no conviction follows. The same state that holds him will examine him for his degree two years later. Which street it happened in, and on what day, nobody wrote down: the night survives in one sentence of his biographer's book and nowhere else at all.
suggested_refs: Athens police detention registers for 1955, which would fix the date and the site of the demonstration
sources: Bob Jessop, Nicos Poulantzas: Marxist Theory and Political Strategy (1985), via the research dossier; not read directly

segments.name: The Navy, the German Detour, and Paris

stops.name: Crete, the navy and the absence without leave
stops.date_confidence: [R] the whole stop is Jessop 1985 via the dossier: the 1957-1960 naval service, the translation-service posting in Athens, the reassignment to Crete after going absent without leave, and the registration with the Athens Lawyers' Association without ever practising. No service record was located. The Crete coordinate is the island's centroid and stands for a posting whose base is not named in any source. Month and day defaulted; 1960 is the closing year of the service rather than a dated event.
stops.campa: Conscription takes him for three years. He starts in the navy's translation service in Athens, a desk job for a man with two languages, and finishes in Crete, reassigned after going absent without leave. On discharge he registers with the Athens Lawyers' Association, as the degree entitles him to do, and never files a case. No service record was located, so what he was doing when he went absent is unknown. The island posting is a punishment, and it is also the longest stretch he will ever spend outside a city.
suggested_refs: Hellenic Navy service records for 1957-1960
Athens Lawyers' Association register of admissions, 1960
sources: Bob Jessop, Nicos Poulantzas: Marxist Theory and Political Strategy (1985), via the research dossier; not read directly

stops.name: Heidelberg, the summer seminars in philosophy of law
stops.date_confidence: [A] Heidelberg as a place of study is confirmed by en.wikipedia and by poulantzas.gr, which lists his formation as 'Athens, Heidelberg and Paris'. Redated: the research pool put the summer seminars in the 'late 1950s', which cannot stand against el.wikipedia's dating of the Munich and Heidelberg seminars in philosophy of law to 1960, after the 1957 degree and the naval service. Month is placed in the seminar season; day defaulted. Coordinate is within roughly 100 m of the Alte Universitaet. [R] the characterisation of what he studied there is inference from the subject of the 1961 memoire, not from a syllabus.
stops.campa: He goes to Germany for the philosophy of law, and Heidelberg is where the summer seminars are. What he sat through in them is nowhere recorded, only that he was in them. The subject is legal idealism with Heidegger somewhere behind it: whether law answers to a nature of things, or only to whoever holds the ministry. It is a conservative discipline in the hands of a Greek whose own police have already held him for a night. Within a year he will write his thesis on exactly that question, in French, in Paris.
suggested_refs: Heidelberg University seminar enrolment lists in Rechtsphilosophie for 1959-1960

stops.name: Munich, the month that ends
stops.date_confidence: [A] that he went to Munich for doctoral study is attested by en.wikipedia, which names the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universitaet, and independently by mixanitouxronou.gr and andro.gr. [R] the month-long stay, the letter to his father, and the stated reason that Nazi ideas remained too influential are Jessop 1985 alone; no letter was located, and Jessop is himself reported to call the reason 'the pretext' without saying what lay behind it. Month and day are an ordering device placing the departure before the Paris arrival; neither is attested. Coordinate is the Geschwister-Scholl-Platz campus.
stops.campa: He arrives at the Ludwig-Maximilians to prepare a doctorate and is gone within about a month. The letter he writes his father gives the reason: Nazi ideas remain too influential here for him to stay. Fifteen years after the war the German faculties are still largely staffed by the men who staffed them during it, and a Greek who was nine years old under the occupation has no appetite for their seminars. He goes to Paris instead. His biographer calls the letter a pretext and does not say what it was a pretext for.
suggested_refs: Poulantzas family correspondence for 1960, which Jessop reports having seen
LMU Munich doctoral registration records for 1960
sources: Bob Jessop (1985) via the research dossier, for the letter

stops.name: Paris, place du Pantheon: the Faculte de droit
stops.date_confidence: [R] the arrival year is genuinely contested and is not resolved here: en.wikipedia says he moved to Paris in 1960 with a teaching assistantship at Pantheon-Sorbonne the same year; poulantzas.gr says he settled in Paris in 1961; el.wikipedia dates the Paris doctorate 1961-64 and the Sorbonne assistantship 1962-1965. This file takes 1961 and leaves the three schemes standing. [R] the charge de cours post in philosophy of law at the Paris law faculty is Jessop 1985 alone: the poulantzas.gr text cited for it in the research pool does not mention such a post at all. Coordinate is the Faculte de droit at 12 place du Pantheon; month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He settles in Paris and finds a place at the law faculty on the place du Pantheon, teaching philosophy of law as a charge de cours while working on his own degree. He is twenty-four, foreign and without money. He will live in this city for the rest of his life and write almost everything in French, about Greece, for readers who mostly are not Greek. On the year he arrived the sources will not agree: one has him here in 1960 with the post already in hand, one in 1961, a third dating the assistantship to 1962.
suggested_refs: Paris Faculte de droit teaching rolls for 1960-1965, which would settle both the post and the arrival year

stops.name: Paris, the memoire on the rebirth of natural law
stops.date_confidence: [A] the memoire, La renaissance du droit naturel en Allemagne apres la Seconde Guerre mondiale, a 161-page typescript of October 1961, is attested by the bibliographic record in the bijus.eu catalogue, cited in the research dossier and not independently reopened on this pass. [R] the Sorbonne as the defending institution and the rue de la Sorbonne coordinate are the pool's reconstruction; no source consulted names the room or the jury. Day defaulted.
stops.campa: He defends a hundred and sixty-one typed pages on the revival of natural law in Germany after the Second World War. The subject is the one Heidelberg and Munich handed him, and it is not an academic subject at all in 1961: German jurists had spent the postwar years arguing that a law standing above statute would have made Nuremberg unnecessary, because the Reich's own statutes were never law. Poulantzas, at twenty-five, is asking whether the argument works.
suggested_refs: The typescript of La renaissance du droit naturel en Allemagne apres la Seconde Guerre mondiale, catalogued at bijus.eu
sources: bijus.eu catalogue entry for the 1961 memoire, via the research dossier

segments.name: Les Temps Modernes and the Turn

stops.name: Paris, Nature des choses et droit
stops.date_confidence: [A] the doctorate Nature des choses et droit: essai sur la dialectique du fait et de la valeur is completed in 1964 and published in 1965 by R. Pichon et R. Durand-Auzias / LGDJ in the Bibliotheque de philosophie du droit, volume V, with a preface by Michel Villey; both facts rest on the publication record cited in the dossier bibliography. The stop is dated to the completion; month and day defaulted. Coordinate is this file's own Faculte de droit pin, used as the institutional venue rather than as a documented location for the defence.
stops.campa: The doctorate is finished: Nature des choses et droit, an essay on the dialectic of fact and value. He is still asking whether the nature of things obliges the judge, and nothing in the book announces the man who will define the state as a condensation of class forces. It appears the following year in the Bibliotheque de philosophie du droit, volume five, with a preface by Michel Villey, the Thomist historian of legal thought. Poulantzas enters print under conservative Catholic patronage.
suggested_refs: Nicos Poulantzas, Nature des choses et droit (Paris: LGDJ, Bibliotheque de philosophie du droit V, 1965), with Michel Villey's preface
James Martin, ed., The Poulantzas Reader: Marxism, Law and the State (Verso, 2008), which brings this material into English
sources: Publication record cited in the research dossier bibliography
versobooks.com, product page for The Poulantzas Reader

stops.name: Gallimard, the younger circle of Les Temps Modernes
stops.date_confidence: [R] the whole stop. That Poulantzas joined the younger contributor circle around Les Temps Modernes alongside Annie Leclerc and Georges Perec, as Simone de Beauvoir records in her memoir, and contributed regularly 1964-66, rests on the dossier's citation of the memoir; the memoir text was not fetched, and the New Left Review obituary cited alongside it in the pool contains no mention of Leclerc at all. The Gallimard coordinate is the corpus value for Editions Gallimard, 5 rue Gaston-Gallimard, inherited byte-identical from simone_de_beauvoir.journey.json and jean_paul_sartre.journey.json; it attests the journal's address, not his presence in the building. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: The journal Jean-Paul Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir founded in 1945 is looking for younger writers, and Beauvoir's memoir names the ones she tried to bring in: Georges Perec, Annie Leclerc, the young Althusserians, and Poulantzas among them. He contributes for three years, and it is here that a philosopher of law learns to write for readers who do not care about law. What he actually printed in those numbers stands unchecked against the tables of contents; only Beauvoir's memoir says he was there at all. Annie Leclerc will become his wife.
suggested_refs: Simone de Beauvoir's memoir, for the passage naming the writers recruited to Les Temps Modernes in 1964
The tables of contents of Les Temps Modernes, 1964-1966, which would fix what Poulantzas actually published there
sources: Research dossier, 'Parisian intellectual formation', citing Beauvoir's memoir
simone_de_beauvoir.journey.json (stop 'Gallimard, the founding of Les Temps Modernes')

stops.name: Paris, rue d'Ulm: Althusser
stops.date_confidence: [R] that Poulantzas met Louis Althusser regularly in Paris and was a close interlocutor of his structuralist Marxism without ever being his formal student rests on the research dossier's general characterisation; no correspondence, seminar list or dated meeting was located. 1966 is an ordering device inside the mid-1960s, month and day defaulted. The rue d'Ulm coordinate is the corpus value for 45 rue d'Ulm, inherited byte-identical from jacques_lacan.journey.json and michel_foucault.journey.json, and stands for the Ecole Normale Superieure as the site of Althusser's teaching, not for a documented visit by Poulantzas.
stops.campa: He meets Louis Althusser through these years and is never his student. What he takes from the rue d'Ulm is a method rather than a doctrine: that a mode of production has levels, that the economic is determinant only in the last instance, and that the last instance never comes. What he does with it is something Althusser never did, which is to turn the apparatus on one object, the capitalist state, and keep turning until the object stops being a thing and becomes a relation.
suggested_refs: Althusser-Poulantzas correspondence in the Althusser papers at IMEC, which would date and characterise the relation
sources: jacques_lacan.journey.json (stop 'Ecole Normale Superieure, salle Dussane: the seminar reopens')

stops.name: Athens, the Second Week of Contemporary Thought
stops.date_confidence: [R] the lecture is Jessop 1985 via the dossier, corroborated only bibliographically by its publication in Marxismos kai Episteme, 1966. The venue within Athens is unknown; the pool used a Zappeion-area placeholder, which is retained here and is explicitly not an attestation. Day defaulted.
stops.campa: He comes home to speak, and what he says in the hall is not what the party wants said. Marxist theories of the state, he argues, have been living off a formula, state monopoly capitalism, which explains the state by dissolving it into the economy and then wonders why it cannot account for anything the state actually does. The class definitions are as rigid as the formula. He is thirty, criticising the orthodoxy of a party he has not joined, in a country eleven months away from a coup.
suggested_refs: Nicos Poulantzas, lecture text as printed in Marxismos kai Episteme (Athens, 1966)
Proceedings or programme of the Second Week of Contemporary Thought, Athens, May 1966, which would fix the venue
sources: Bob Jessop (1985) via the research dossier; not read directly

stops.name: Paris, quai Anatole-France: the CNRS
stops.date_confidence: [A] the CNRS appointment as attache de recherche in law, 1966-1972, and the deputy editorship of the Archives de philosophie du droit, 1966-1969, are institutional and bibliographic record. Contradiction named rather than buried: andro.gr gives the CNRS start as 1965, en.wikipedia as 1966; this file takes 1966 with en.wikipedia and the dossier. Coordinate is approximate and is a period placeholder only: it sits roughly 250 m south of 15 quai Anatole-France, and CNRS headquarters today is at 3 rue Michel-Ange in the 16e. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He is appointed attache de recherche in law at the Centre national de la recherche scientifique and holds the post six years, the whole span in which he stops being a philosopher of law and becomes a theorist of the state. The same year he takes the deputy editorship of the Archives de philosophie du droit. He is thirty and has published one book, about natural law. The French state is paying a Greek exile a research salary to work out what a state is. On the year the salary began the sources split: 1965 in one account, 1966 in another.
suggested_refs: CNRS personnel files for the law section, 1966-1972
Archives de philosophie du droit, mastheads for 1966-1969
sources: Institutional and bibliographic record cited in the research dossier

stops.name: Paris, the marriage to Annie Leclerc
stops.date_confidence: [A] the marriage to Annie Leclerc in 1966 is independently attested by andro.gr and mixanitouxronou.gr and confirmed by en.wikipedia and el.wikipedia. [R] the exact day, 6 December, is Jessop 1985 alone. [R] the 1963 meeting given in the research pool as [A] is downgraded: the Hall obituary cited for it, fetched in full, does not mention Leclerc at any point, and the date is Jessop-only. The ceremony venue is unrecorded in every source consulted and the coordinate is a generic central-Paris placeholder.
stops.campa: He marries Annie Leclerc, writer and philosopher, whom the journal circle brought him. She will publish Parole de femme in 1974 and become one of the voices of the difference current in French feminism; he will publish four books on classes and the state inside the same decade. They have one daughter. Where the ceremony took place is recorded nowhere reachable, which is a small odd loss in a life otherwise so heavily written up. The day, the sixth of December, comes from his biographer and from nowhere else.
suggested_refs: Paris municipal marriage registers for 6 December 1966, which would name the arrondissement and the witnesses

segments.name: The Colonels, the Split, and May

stops.name: Paris, the committee of Greeks against the dictatorship
stops.date_confidence: [A] the coup of 21 April 1967 is established historical record. [R] that Poulantzas was a founding member of the anti-dictatorship committee of Greeks in Paris and wrote party journalism under the pseudonym N. Skyrianos is Jessop 1985 alone, via the dossier; no committee papers and no Skyrianos byline were located. The committee's meeting address is unknown and the coordinate is a Left Bank placeholder.
stops.campa: The colonels take Athens before dawn on the twenty-first of April, and by evening the Greek exile in Paris has stopped being a career choice and become a political condition. Poulantzas is a founding member of the anti-dictatorship committee of Greeks in the city. He writes for the party press as N. Skyrianos, pushing the analysis leftward against a leadership that reads the coup as an accident of generals rather than as a form the capitalist state can take when hegemony fails.
suggested_refs: Papers of the anti-dictatorship committee of Greeks in Paris, 1967-1974
KKE Interior party press for 1967-1974, for pieces signed N. Skyrianos
sources: Bob Jessop (1985) via the research dossier; not read directly

stops.name: Paris, the party splits in two
stops.date_confidence: [A] that he joined and remained a member of the Communist Party of the Interior after the split is attested verbatim by Stuart Hall in New Left Review I/119, in the words quoted. Contradiction flagged and deliberately not resolved: Hall places the split 'in the wake of the Colonel's coup' and the KKE's 12th Plenum formalised it in February 1968, months before the Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia that August, whereas en.wikipedia's article on the KKE (Interior) says the split followed that invasion. The research pool asserted the invasion as the cause, which the February date will not support; this file dates the stop to the plenum and lets both accounts stand. Day defaulted; the Paris coordinate is generic, the split being an exile-wide event with no single address.
stops.campa: The Greek Communist Party breaks apart in exile, and Poulantzas goes with the wing that will be called the Party of the Interior: anti-Stalinist, Eurocommunist before the word, arguing for a road to socialism that runs through elections rather than around them. He stays a member for the rest of his life. Hall dates the break to the aftermath of the colonels' coup; other accounts hang it on the tanks entering Prague that August. The plenum that formalised it met in February.
stops.quote: After the internal split, in the wake of the Colonel's coup, he joined, and remained, a member of the Greek Communist Party of the Interior
stops.quote_source: Stuart Hall, 'Nicos Poulantzas: State, Power, Socialism', New Left Review I/119 (January-February 1980)
suggested_refs: Minutes of the KKE 12th Plenum, February 1968
en.wikipedia, 'Communist Party of Greece (Interior)', for the competing account of the split's cause

stops.name: Rue Saint-Severin, Maspero publishes Pouvoir politique et classes sociales
stops.date_confidence: [A] Pouvoir politique et classes sociales de l'Etat capitaliste is published by Maspero in Paris in 1968 (en.wikipedia, fr.wikipedia; kathimerini.gr notes the coincidence with the May events). [R] the two details that always travel with it, that it appeared days before the occupation of the Sorbonne and that students bought several thousand copies during the upheaval, are Jessop 1985 alone: no fetched source gives the book's month of publication, let alone its sales. The month here is therefore an ordering device, not an attestation. The coordinate is the Latin Quarter address of Maspero's bookshop La Joie de Lire and is approximate to the publishing milieu rather than to an office.
stops.campa: Francois Maspero publishes Pouvoir politique et classes sociales de l'Etat capitaliste, four hundred pages arguing that the state is not an instrument the ruling class picks up but a structure with its own relative autonomy, which serves capital best precisely when no capitalist is holding it. The Latin Quarter is about to be barricaded. The tradition says the book was days ahead of the Sorbonne occupation and that students carried it off the tables by the thousand. The tradition has one source.
suggested_refs: Bibliographie de la France for 1968, which would give the depot legal month of the Maspero edition and settle the May question
sources: Bob Jessop (1985) via the research dossier, for the May-1968 proximity and the sales

segments.name: Vincennes and the Debate on the State

stops.name: Vincennes, the department in the woods
stops.date_confidence: [A] that Poulantzas was among the first sociology faculty at the experimental university at Vincennes, later Paris VIII, and taught there until his death is attested through the dossier and Michael Lowy's Verso memorial piece. [A] fr.wikipedia gives the campus its first students in January 1969, on 40,000 square metres of the Bois de Vincennes belonging to the City of Paris, and records its demolition on 27-29 August 1980 with no trace remaining on the site. Coordinate: the research pool carried two Vincennes points 1.1 km apart (48.8342/2.4423 and 48.8433/2.4381), neither verifiable; this file inherits the atlas's canonical Vincennes pin byte-identical from michel_foucault.journey.json, gilles_deleuze.journey.json, felix_guattari.journey.json and jacques_lacan.journey.json, and labels it approximate. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: The state builds an experimental university in the Bois de Vincennes out of prefabricated blocks, to absorb the students May produced and to keep them somewhere it can see them. Poulantzas is among the first sociology faculty and stays a decade, to the end of his life. There is no entrance requirement worth the name and the rooms fill with people enrolled nowhere. He is teaching the theory of the state inside a building the state put up as a containment measure.
suggested_refs: Founding appointment lists of the Vincennes sociology department, 1968-1969
Photographs of the demolition of the Vincennes campus, 27-29 August 1980
sources: versobooks.com/blogs/news/1908, Michael Lowy, 'The Nicos Poulantzas I Knew'

stops.name: Vincennes, the little duo
stops.date_confidence: [A] Michael Lowy became Poulantzas's assistant in 1969, replacing Emir Sader, and the two taught together on the Third International, the national question, state theory, Lenin and Gramsci; Lowy's own words for the arrangement are quoted. Correction recorded: the research pool attributed to this same source the sentences 'Poulantzas taught at Universite de Paris 8-Vincennes, where he worked with Michael Lowy from 1969-1977' and 'classes were packed to the rafters'. Neither phrase is in the fetched piece. They are fabrications and are dropped. Month and day are an ordering device for the start of the academic year, not an attestation. Coordinate inherited from this file's own Vincennes pin.
stops.campa: Michael Lowy becomes his teaching assistant, replacing Emir Sader, and the two of them run courses together on the Third International, the national question, Lenin, Gramsci, the state. They disagree in front of the students and make no attempt to hide it, which is the pedagogy: two Marxists arguing where the class can watch. Lowy will remember him afterwards not as the depressive of the legend but as warm, funny, generous, a Marxist full of joy.
stops.quote: Our little duo lasted for some years.
stops.quote_source: Michael Lowy, 'The Nicos Poulantzas I Knew', Verso Books blog, 5 March 2015
suggested_refs: Michael Lowy, 'The Nicos Poulantzas I Knew', versobooks.com/blogs/news/1908
Paris VIII course listings in sociology, 1969-1979

stops.name: London, New Left Review: the problem of the capitalist state
stops.date_confidence: [A] 'The Problem of the Capitalist State', New Left Review I/58 (1969), reviewing Ralph Miliband's The State in Capitalist Society, is attested by the article itself, fetched at newleftreview.org; the quoted sentence is verbatim from it. [R] no source confirms that Poulantzas ever visited the New Left Review office: the Carlisle Street coordinate stands for the place of publication and nothing more. Miliband has no file in this atlas, so the debate is carried here as a one-directional citation on Poulantzas's own stop and is not staged as anyone else's scene. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He reviews Ralph Miliband's The State in Capitalist Society for New Left Review, calls it of capital importance, and then takes it apart. Miliband has answered bourgeois political science by counting who sits on which board, and in doing so has accepted the ground the question was asked on. The state is not the men inside it. Behind the quarrel is an absence Poulantzas names openly: Karl Marx wrote three volumes on the economic level and no book on the state, and a century of Marxists have filled the hole with whatever came to hand.
stops.quote: Marx thus concentrated on the economic level of the capitalist mode of production, and did not deal specifically with the other levels such as the State.
stops.quote_source: Nicos Poulantzas, 'The Problem of the Capitalist State', New Left Review I/58 (1969)

Poulantzas reads Mussolini's Italy and Hitler's Germany not as madness and not as a lapse of civilisation but as exceptional forms of the capitalist state, thrown up when the bourgeoisie's hegemony breaks and the ordinary parliamentary form can no longer hold the classes together. The book is also an indictment of the Comintern, which had the analysis available, chose social fascism instead, and lost Germany with it.

stops.name: London, the argument crosses the Channel
stops.date_confidence: [A] Political Power and Social Classes, translated by Timothy O'Hagan, is published by New Left Books in 1973; 'On Social Classes' appears in New Left Review I/78 the same year and was fetched directly. stops.campa: New Left Books publishes Political Power and Social Classes in Timothy O'Hagan's translation, five years after the French, and the same year New Left Review carries On Social Classes. Between them the argument crosses the Channel in a single season. English-speaking Marxism has been quarrelling about the state without much to quarrel with, and now has the whole structural apparatus in its own language. What arrives with it is a definition of class that will not reduce to income.
stops.quote: We can thus say that a social class is defined by its place in the ensemble of social practices, i.e. by its place in the ensemble of the division of labour which includes political and ideological relations.
stops.quote_source: Nicos Poulantzas, 'On Social Classes', New Left Review I/78 (1973)

stops.campa: Les classes sociales dans le capitalisme aujourd'hui asks the question that decides everything about strategy in the West: who are all these people. Technicians, engineers, supervisors, clerks, teachers, the whole salaried mass that neither owns nor produces surplus value. He calls them the new petty bourgeoisie, a class defined by its place in mental labour and supervision rather than by its payslip. The book also names an internal bourgeoisie: native capital that is neither comprador nor autonomous, a third term the existing vocabulary had no room for.

stops.name: London, the reply to Miliband and Laclau
stops.date_confidence: [A] 'The Capitalist State: A Reply to Miliband and Laclau', New Left Review I/95 (1976), fetched directly; both quoted passages are verbatim from it. The bracketed completion of the book title in the defence against abstractionism is supplied for clarity, the fetched text having trimmed it. Month and day defaulted. stops.campa: Seven years into the quarrel he answers Miliband and Ernesto Laclau in one article, and the tone has changed. The charge is abstractionism: that his state has no history in it and no struggle. He rejects the charge, pointing to the pages where the class struggle is on every one, and then concedes something larger, which is that he and the Althusserians held the theoretical process so firmly apart from the concrete that they never worked out how the concrete gets in.
stops.quote: What we failed to see at the time was that, while firmly upholding the specificity of the theoretical process in relation to the 'concrete real', we should have perceived the particular way in which this 'real' intervenes.
stops.quote_source: Nicos Poulantzas, 'The Capitalist State: A Reply to Miliband and Laclau', New Left Review I/95 (1976)

stops.name: Athens, the junta falls and the papers reopen
stops.date_confidence: [A] the collapse of the Greek junta in July 1974 and of the Portuguese Estado Novo in April 1974 are established historical record; 24 July 1974 is the date of the metapolitefsi and is supplied as an ordering device, the research pool giving only the year. [R] no source consulted attests a physical visit to Athens in 1974; the Athens pin stands for where his Greek-language writing appeared.
stops.campa: Cyprus breaks the colonels and they hand the country back. Within months Poulantzas is writing in Avgi, Ta Nea, To Vima and Anti, arguing in Greek for the first time in years to a readership that can now read him legally. Which pieces he actually filed, and in which of the four papers, nobody has checked against the bound volumes. Portugal's Estado Novo went in April; Spain's caudillo is dying. Three Southern European dictatorships end inside eighteen months, and the man who theorised the exceptional state watches all three go while they are still going.
suggested_refs: Bound volumes of Avgi, Ta Nea, To Vima and Anti for 1974-1979, which would establish the extent of his Greek journalism

stops.name: Paris, Maspero: La crise des dictatures
stops.date_confidence: [A] La crise des dictatures: Portugal, Grece, Espagne, Maspero, Paris, 1975, with a revised second edition in 1976, is attested by the publication record. Portugal, Greece, Spain in one book, three regimes falling not because they were beaten from outside but because the ruling blocs inside them came apart. It is the internal bourgeoisie doing it, native capital that has outgrown the dictatorship's usefulness to it. The events move faster than the printer can set them and a revised second edition follows within a year. He writes up Lisbon and Madrid without going to either. No source consulted places him in Portugal or Spain at any point in his life.

stops.date_confidence: [A] the exchange is attested by the Verso Books blog piece 'A Revolutionary from the OECD: The Castoriadis-Poulantzas Debate', fetched directly, which dates Poulantzas's article to Avgi of 1 January 1977. stops.name: Paris, PUF: L'Etat, le pouvoir, le socialisme
stops.date_confidence: [A] L'Etat, le pouvoir, le socialisme, Presses Universitaires de France, Paris, 1978, is attested by the publication record, and the definition of the state as a material condensation of a relationship of forces among classes and class fractions is corroborated as his formulation across multiple secondary sources, including the transform! anniversary essay of 2019, which quotes it. Month and day defaulted. Coordinate is PUF's historic boulevard Saint-Germain address and is approximate, as at the 1976 stop.
stops.campa: The last book. The state, he writes, is a material condensation of a relationship of forces among classes and class fractions, which means it is not a thing, not a subject and not an instrument, but the shape a struggle takes when it settles into offices and statutes. And he names what he sees coming in the Western democracies: authoritarian statism, the steady drift of power from parliaments to executives and administrations, with the forms of liberty left standing and hollowed.

stops.name: London, towards a democratic socialism
stops.date_confidence: [A] 'Towards a Democratic Socialism', New Left Review I/109 (1978), fetched directly; the quoted sentence is verbatim from its opening critique. Warning recorded, because the pool's other quotation from this article invites the error: the line about 'the sweeping replacement of formal representative democracy by the real, direct democracy of workers' councils' is Poulantzas characterising the classical Leninist position in order to reject it, and is not his own prescription. Month and day defaulted; the coordinate is the New Left Review office as place of publication.
stops.campa: New Left Review carries his account of the two roads and his refusal of both. Social democracy has managed the state and never touched it; Leninism has proposed smashing it and replacing representative institutions wholesale with councils. Both, he says, distrust the initiative of the masses, which is a strange charge to lay against revolutionaries and exactly the one he means. What he wants instead is representative democracy and direct democracy at once, with neither dissolved into the other.
stops.quote: Both are marked by statism and profound distrust of mass initiatives, in short by suspicion of democratic demands.
stops.quote_source: Nicos Poulantzas, 'Towards a Democratic Socialism', New Left Review I/109 (1978)
suggested_refs: Nicos Poulantzas, 'Towards a Democratic Socialism', New Left Review I/109 (1978), read whole, against the misquotation of the workers' council passage

stops.name: Paris, the window
stops.date_confidence: [A] the date, the city, the manner and the age are secure: en.wikipedia, 'died by suicide in Paris on 3 October 1979, at the age of 43'; ertnews.gr, 'aftoktonise stis 3 Oktovriou 1979 sto Parisi'; Hall, New Left Review I/119, 'The unexpected and tragic death of Nicos Poulantzas, in Paris, in October of this year'. [A] the Tsoucalas account of the books thrown from the window is relayed by Michael Lowy in the Verso piece, fetched, together with the depression and a 1978 'accident'. [R] the site is genuinely unresolved and has four horns: 13th floor of his own apartment building (andro.gr, mixanitouxronou.gr); 22nd floor of the Tour Montparnasse (English-language tradition, corroborated by nothing fetched); 29th floor of a Paris apartment building (a contemporaneous Greek notice preserved by Kathimerini, whose page returned a fetch error); 50th floor of the Tour Montparnasse in the 13e arrondissement (fr.wikipedia), which is self-contradictory since the tower stands in the 15e. A hypothesis worth recording without adopting: '13th floor' may be a corruption of '13e arrondissement'. The research pool plotted the death at 48.8421/2.3219, which is exactly the Tour Montparnasse and stakes the map on the least-supported variant; this file refuses that and uses a neutral central-Paris point. [gap] no grave, tomb, cemetery or funeral arrangement is documented in poulantzas.gr, mixanitouxronou.gr or the Lowy piece, all of which cover the death in detail.
stops.campa: He goes out of a high window and dies. Constantine Tsoucalas, said to have been there, remembered him throwing his books out first, saying the work was worthless. Which building it was, and which floor, no two accounts agree: the thirteenth of his own block, the twenty-second of the Tour Montparnasse, the twenty-ninth of some apartment building, the fiftieth of a tower that stands in a different arrondissement from the one the account puts it in. No grave is recorded anywhere. He was forty-three.

stops.name: London, Verso: the books come back
stops.date_confidence: [A] Verso reissued Fascism and Dictatorship, trans. Judith White, in January 2019 with a new foreword by Dylan Riley, framed on the publisher's own page around 'the resurgence of the far right across Europe and the emergence of the alt-right in the US'; The Poulantzas Reader, ed. James Martin, appeared April 2008; The Crisis of the Dictatorships has stayed in the Verso catalogue since 1976. All three from versobooks.com product pages, fetched. Day defaulted. stops.campa: His English publisher reissues Fascism and Dictatorship with a new foreword by Dylan Riley, and the framing on the jacket is not historical.
